"It's a long story," the old man began, leaning back and closing his eyes, "but I can tell you the essentials in a few words. It all goes back to the Ballarat gold-fields in Australia, in the early sixties. I was a young man then, full of fire and with little conscience, and I became the leader of a gang of bushrangers. We were known as the Ballarat Gang, and we committed many a bold robbery. One day we waylaid the gold convoy from the mines to the coast. There was a fight, and though we got the gold, several men were killed. I was the only one who escaped with the loot and made my way to Europe, where I changed my name and began a new life as a respectable man. I had hoped that my past was buried forever, until one day, years later, I encountered Charles McCarthy in London. He had been a wagon-driver in that very convoy, and he recognized me at once. From that moment, I was a slave to his blackmail, and my life became a misery of his making."

"It's a long story," the old man said; "it goes back to the days of the gold-fields in Australia, when I was a young man and full of the devil. I was the leader of the Ballarat Gang—Black Jack of Ballarat they called me. We were a lawless lot, and we held up the gold convoys from the mines. One day, we struck a particularly rich haul, but it was a bloody business. McCarthy was the wagon driver. He was the only one we spared, though I didn't know then that I was sparing a man who would be a curse to me for the rest of my life. I came back to England with my fortune, changed my name, and sought to live a decent life for the sake of my girl. But McCarthy found me out. He had followed my trail, and he settled down on my land like a leech, sucking my lifeblood with his threats and his demands, until I could endure it no longer."

"It's a long story, and yet it is a short one too," said Turner. "I'll tell you the truth of it, for I've no reason to lie now, and I'd like the girl to think of me as a man who was driven to it, rather than a cold-blooded murderer. You've heard of the Ballarat Gang, I suppose? We were a dozen of us in the early days of the gold fever, and we lived by our wits and our revolvers. I was the leader, and we had a good run of it until the day we stuck up the gold convoy from Ballarat. There was a man there—a driver—who begged for his life, and I, being a young fool, spared him. That man was Charles McCarthy. He knew my face then, and he never forgot it. Years later, when I had come back to England a wealthy man and was trying to live down the past, he turned up like a ghost from the grave. He had nothing, and I had everything. He knew he could hang me with a word, and from that day on, I was his slave and his bank."

"It's a long story, sir," he said; "and one which it is hard to
tell, but I will give it to you as short as I can. You do not
know what a fiend that man McCarthy has been to me. For twenty
years he has gripped me by the throat, and he has made my life a
hell upon earth. I was a happy man, a rich man, and a respected
man, until he came back to me out of the past and laid his cold
hand upon my shoulder. I will tell you how it all began, and you
will see if I am a murderer or a man who has but done an act of
justice."

"It’s a long story," said the old man; "it goes back to the early days in the Australian bush. I was a young man then, with more blood in my veins than brains in my head. I fell in with a bad crowd, and before I knew it I was one of the Ballarat Gang. We were six in all, and we lived by our wits and our rifles. One day we stuck up the gold escort on its way from the mines. There was a fight, and the two troopers were killed. I was the one who held the horses, but I was as guilty as the rest. McCarthy was the driver of that escort, and he was the only man who saw my face clearly and lived to tell the tale. I spared him then, but I have paid for that mercy a thousand times over in the years that followed."

"It's as well," said the old man; "it's a question whether I
shall live to the Assizes, so it matters little to me, but I
should wish to spare Alice the shock. And now I will make the
thing clear to you; it has been a long time in the acting, but
will not take me long to tell.

It was in the early '60s at the diggings. I was a young chap then, hot-blooded and reckless, ready to turn my hand to anything. I got among bad companions, and we were soon doing things that we shouldn't. We were the Ballarat Gang—there were six of us—and we held up the gold escort from Ballarat to Melbourne. We were successful, and the gold was ours, but there was blood on it. McCarthy was a driver on that escort, and he was the only man who survived our attack. I can see him now, cowering under the seat as we ransacked the mailbags. I spared his life, and I have lived to rue the day. I made my way to England with my share of the spoils, changed my name, and settled down to a life of peace and respectability. I thought I was safe, but the past is a shadow that follows a man to his grave.

"It was in the early '60s at the diggings. I was a young chap then, free-handed and lawless, and I fell in with a set of men who were as reckless as myself. We formed what was known in those days as the Ballarat Gang. There were six of us, and we made the roads unsafe between the mines and the coast. We were not common thieves, or so we thought ourselves, but we took what we wanted from those who had more than enough. One day we received intelligence of a large gold-escort which was to pass through a certain gully on its way to Melbourne. We lay in wait for it and we moved to the attack. The police-escort was shot down, and the gold was ours. Among those who survived the encounter was the driver of the wagon, a man named Charles McCarthy. I can see his face now as he looked up at me from the dust, pleading for his life. I had never been a man of blood, and I held my hand, letting him go free with his life, though I little knew then that I was sparing the very man who would one day become my ruin."

"It was in the early '60s at the diggings. I was a young chap then, wild, reckless, ready for anything. I fell in with a bad crowd, and, as the saying goes, one thing led to another until we took to the bush. There were six of us in the gang, and a lawless, murderous lot we were. We used to waylay the gold-escorts on their way from the mines to the coast. One day, near Ballarat, we attacked a convoy that was particularly well-guarded. There was a fierce battle, and many lives were lost on both sides. In the end, we captured the gold, but I was the only one who showed any mercy. I held my hand when it came to the driver of the wagon, a man who sat cowering upon his seat. That man was Charles McCarthy."

"It was in the early '60's at the diggings. I was a young chap then, hot-blooded and reckless, ready to turn my hand to anything. I got among bad companions, and before I knew it, I was one of the Ballarat Gang. There were six of us, and we had a wild time of it, sticking up stations and robbing the gold escorts. One day we attacked the convoy from Ballarat to Melbourne. We shot the police, but spared the driver, though he had seen our faces and could have sworn to every one of us. That driver was this man, Charles McCarthy. I can see his face now, as he looked up at me with those cold, calculating eyes while I stood over him with my revolver, little dreaming that I was sparing the man who was to dog me to my grave."

"It was in the early '60s at the diggings. I was a young chap then, hot-blooded and reckless, ready to turn my hand to anything. I got among bad companions, and before I knew it, I was the leader of a gang of bushrangers. We were the Ballarat Gang, and we made a name for ourselves that is still remembered in the colony. One day we received word of a gold escort coming from Ballarat to Melbourne, and we laid an ambush for it. There were six of us, and we swept down upon the convoy. The troopers fought well, but we were too many for them. We killed two, and the rest fled, leaving the gold in our hands. Among those who escaped was the driver of the wagon, a man named Charles McCarthy. I had my gun levelled at him, but I could not find the heart to pull the trigger on a man who looked me so straight in the eyes. I let him go, and that was the greatest mistake of my life."

"It was in the early '60's at the diggings. I was a young chap
then, hot-blooded and reckless, ready to turn my hand at
anything; I got among bad companions, took to drink, had no luck
with my claim, took to the bush, and in a word became what you
would call over here a highway robber. There were six of us, and
we had a wild, free life of it, sticking up a station from time
to time, or stopping the wagons on the road to the diggings.
Black Jack of Ballarat was the name I went under, and our party
is still remembered in the colony as the Ballarat Gang.

"He knew me again, for his memory was as long as his life. I
thought that I should like to help him, and as he was an old
friend and I had plenty of money, I was quite willing to do it.
He soon let me see, however, that he was going to be my master.
He began to borrow large sums of money from me, and he brought
over his son and his servants and his trap and his horses, and he
expected to be treated as a gentleman and to have as much of
everything as I had myself. He became my tenant at Hatherley
Farm, and as long as I could pay him what he asked I thought that
he would be satisfied. But he was not. He soon found out that he
could hold me in his power, and then he was never happy unless he
was making me feel it. And so things went on until the end came."

"And what was it?" asked Holmes.

"Well, it was the same old story. He wanted my girl to marry his
son. He had heard that she was to be my heiress, and he thought
it would be a very good thing for his boy. He knew that I should
never allow it, for his son was as bad as he was, but he thought
he could force me to it. I refused, as you may imagine, and that
led to the quarrel. I met him by appointment at the Boscombe
Pool, where he told me that unless I agreed to his terms he would
reveal my secret. I was a desperate man, and I knew that if he
spoke it would be the ruin of my life and the disgrace of my
daughter. I saw him standing there, with his back turned towards
me, and I could not help it. I struck him with a stone that lay
upon the grass, and then I went away into the woods. I heard his
son's cry, but I was too far off to see him. That is the whole
truth of the matter, and I am ready to sign it."

"It's a very sad story," said Holmes. "I shall keep your
confession, and only use it if it is needed. In the meantime, I
will do my best for young McCarthy."

"God bless you!" said the old man. "I have not long to live, and
I should like to die in peace."

He signed the paper which Holmes had written out, and then
shuffled out of the room, a broken and dying man.

"Well, Watson," said Holmes, as he folded up the paper and put it
into his pocket, "I think that we have done a good day's work.
I shall go back to London to-night, and you may come with me if
you like."

"I shall be glad to do so," I answered.

"Then we will have our dinner and start. I have no doubt that
Lestrade will be surprised when he hears the result of our
investigations."

And so ended the mystery of Boscombe Valley. James McCarthy was
acquitted at the Assizes, and John Turner died only a few weeks
later. The secret of his crime was never revealed, and he was
laid to rest in the quiet little churchyard of Ross, with no one
to suspect the dark secret which had shadowed his life. Alice and
James were married not long after, and I have no doubt that they
are still living happily together in the beautiful valley which
was the scene of so much sorrow and mystery.

"He came up and spoke to me. 'I've been looking for you this long
time, Black Jack,' he said. 'I've tracked you down at last, and
now you've got to make my fortune. It's only fair that you should
share with me, considering that I've been a poor man all my life,
and that I was the one who saw you and the others in that
Ballarat affair.'

"Well, I was a rich man and he was a poor one, so I thought I
might as well help him. I gave him money and brought him down
here, and I let him have Hatherley Farm for nothing, and
presented him with horses and a trap, and did everything I could
to make him comfortable. But his grip was upon me, and it grew
tighter and tighter, until it seemed to choke me. He made my life
a burden, and he began to talk to me as if I were his servant
instead of his benefactor. Then he must have his son to live with
him, and he began to talk about a marriage between the two young
folks. Alice didn't want it and James didn't want it, but
McCarthy was determined that it should be, and he wouldn't listen
to a word against it. He knew that I'd do anything sooner than
have my secret told, and he meant to make the most of his
knowledge. I could see that he was as much a villain as ever, and
it seemed to me that it was better that one of us should go to
the wall than that we should both be ruined. I had determined in
my mind to have a talk with him, but on the afternoon when I met
him at the Boscombe Pool he had already had a talk with James,
which had led to high words. He was waiting for me there, for I
had an appointment with him, but he thought that it was his son
who was coming, and so he gave the old signal of 'Cooee!' which we
used to use in Australia. When he saw me he began to abuse me,
and to tell me what he'd do if I didn't give in to him. Then my
old blood boiled within me, and I felt that I could stand it no
longer. I picked up a heavy stone and struck him with it from
behind. I didn't mean to kill him, but I was a strong man then,
and the blow was a heavy one. I stood and looked at him for a
few minutes, and then I saw his son coming through the trees. I
managed to hide myself behind a big beech-tree until the young
man had gone for help, and then I made my way home. That is the
truth of the matter, and I'll sign it now if you'll let me."

"He had me in his power from the first. He knew me at once, and
I saw he meant to live on me for the rest of my days. I was weak,
and I gave him money, and I gave him Hatherley Farm. But it was
not enough. He must have all he could get, and I had a girl to
provide for. He had a son, too, and he must have him marry my
girl. That was the last straw. I had lived in hell since first I
met him. My life was at his mercy. Now he would have my Alice,
and I'd rather see her in her grave first.

"We met by appointment at the Boscombe Pool. He was there and I
told him my mind. He only laughed. He had no more pity than a
stone. Then the son came. McCarthy, senior, called to him to
wait, and then they had words. I stood behind a tree and watched
them. I saw the boy leave, and then the old man, instead of
returning, sat down upon a log by the edge of the water. My heart
was full of bitterness. It was him or me. I could not stand his
tyranny no longer. I picked up a stone and I struck him down. I
did not mean to kill him, but he died. I took my cloak, which I
had dropped when I ran out, and I made my way home through the
wood. That is the truth. I will sign anything you like."

"He had been in the Victorian police, and had lost his billet for
his bad ways. He had come over here, and was at his last penny.
He knew me at once and was not slow to use his knowledge. He
followed me home and soon became the master of my house and of my
peace. I gave him Hatherley Farm and I paid his bills and let him
live on me. But even that was not enough. He grew more and more
exacting, and for a long time I was in his power. At last it came
to a head. He told me that his son and my daughter must marry. I
refused, and we had a desperate quarrel. He swore that he would
have me arrested if I didn't give way, and I told him to do his
worst. But it broke my heart to think of my Alice. I knew how the
shame of such a father would break her life. I determined to end
it. I took my gun and went down to the pool to wait for him.
There I saw him and his son, and I heard them quarrelling. When
the son left him I saw my chance. I picked up a stone and I
struck him a blow upon the head, and then I went away as fast as
I could. But when I got home I heard that the son had been
arrested, and then I knew that I must speak out. But I wanted to
see you first, and to tell you all. I knew you were a clever man
and would find it out, and I wanted you to know that I had not
meant to let the young man come to harm."

"I am glad you have told me," said Holmes. "I shall use your
statement only if it is needed. And now I must go back to London,
for I have much work to do."

"And what will you do about young McCarthy?"

"I think that I can manage to get him off."

"God bless you!" said the old man.

He rose from the sofa and limped out of the room, his head bowed
upon his chest.

"Well, Watson," said Holmes as the door closed behind him, "I
think that we have done a good day's work. Let us go and see if
we can find a train to London."

The next morning we were back in Baker Street, and Holmes was
busy with his chemical experiments, while I was reading a book
upon the Afghan war.

"I think, Watson," said he, looking up from his test-tube, "that
we have cleared up that little mystery in Boscombe Valley. Young
McCarthy is free, and I hear that he and Miss Turner are to be
married. I am glad of it, for they are both good young people.
As for old Turner, he died a few days after we left, so that his
secret is safe with us."

"And Lestrade?" I asked.

"Oh, Lestrade is quite happy. He has got his conviction, and he
thinks that he is a very clever fellow. I have not told him the
truth, for it would only make him unhappy, and it would do no
good to anyone. And now, Watson, if you will excuse me, I must
get on with my work, for I have a very interesting case in hand
concerning a royal personage and a certain photograph."

"He had spent his money, and he was as bad as a man can be. He
caught me by the arm, and he looked me in the face, and he
whispered to me, 'So you're the Black Jack of Ballarat. You don't
forget me, do you? No, and I haven't forgotten you.' I knew that
he would have my life in his hands.

"I tried to shake him off, but it was no use. He told me that he
would have the law on me if I didn't come to his terms. He was as
bitter and as hard as a man could be.

"I had to take him and his son in with me. I gave them Hatherley
Farm and let them have all they wanted. Still it was not enough.
He wanted more and more, and I had to give it. Then he began to
talk of our children marrying. He knew that I wouldn't have it,
and he knew that it would be a bitter pill for me. But I had to
keep him quiet, so I didn't say no.

"But then things went further. He wanted more than that. He
wanted me to give him the Hall, and all that I had. He told me
that he would tell the whole story if I didn't. I couldn't stand
it any longer. I'm a dying man, as I told you, and I didn't want
to leave my girl in his power. So I made up my mind. I took my
gun and my dog and I went out to the Boscombe Pool. I knew that
he was to be there. I waited behind the tree and I saw him and
his son together. I saw them quarrel, and I saw the son go away.
Then I came out and I killed him. I killed him with a stone that
lay upon the ground. It was a quick death and a merciful one. I
had my old cloak with me, and I threw it over him and then I
walked away. I didn't think that anyone had seen me. I didn't
know that his son had come back.

"And now you know the truth. You can do what you like with it.
I'm a dying man, and it matters little to me. But I would have
given my life to save the boy if it had come to that."

The old man's head sank upon his breast, and he sat silent for a
time. Holmes rose and went over to him, laying his hand upon his
shoulder.

"I will keep your secret," he said. "Young McCarthy is safe, and
no one shall ever know the truth from me. You have suffered enough
in your life, and I will not be the one to bring more upon you."

The old man looked up at him with a look of gratitude in his eyes.
"Thank you," he said. "God bless you for that."

He rose from the sofa and limped slowly from the room. We heard
his heavy step upon the stairs and then the closing of the door
below.

"A strange case, Watson," said Holmes as he reached for his
pipe. "A strange case, and a sad one. But justice has been done,
and no one is the worse for it. And now let us have a cup of tea
and then we can catch the evening train to London."

The "Boscombe Valley Mystery" was over. Young McCarthy was
released from prison, and he and Alice Turner were married not
long after. The secret of the murder was never revealed, and
John Turner died a few weeks after our visit. It was one of the
most singular cases that I ever had the privilege of witnessing,
and I shall never forget the look upon the old man's face as he
told us his story.

"'Here we are, Jack,' says he, touching me on the arm; 'we'll be
as good as a family to you. There's two of us, me and my son, and
you can have the keeping of us. If you don't--it's a fine,
law-abiding country is England, and there's always a policeman
within hail.'

"It was a thing I would not listen to, and I told him so. And
still he insisted, and I believe he would have had his way but
for my daughter herself, who would have none of it. Still, I knew
it must come to a head one way or another, and I knew that if it
came to a question between his son and my Alice I should be firm
as a rock. The end was to come soon. I found out from his own son
that he had gone down to Boscombe Pool to meet someone. He didn't
know who it was, but I knew, and I had a mind to see what he
intended to do with me.

"Well, I reached the spot before he came, and I sat behind the
tree until I heard him. He was standing there with his back to
me, and he didn't even hear me come. I stood there and watched
them, he and his son, and then I heard him goading the boy to ask
my Alice's hand. I heard the boy's answer, and I heard the
father's cruel, heartless retort. I could bear it no longer, and
I rushed out. Before I knew it I had struck him, and he fell. I
didn't mean to kill him, God knows, but he was a dead man as he
touched the ground.

"Well, there's my story. I've told you all. I don't know what
you'll do with me, but I've told the truth at last."

"I am not your judge," said Sherlock Holmes. "You have cleared
an innocent man, and that is what I wanted. As for the rest, you
must answer to your own conscience. Watson, I think that we have
finished our work here. We may go back to London by the night
train."

"I wouldn't have it. I'd have seen her dead first. He said I
might as well give way at once, for that he would have her
married to his son, and that he would go through with it even to
his own destruction if I would not. 'It's a fine thing for me,
Jack,' says he, 'to be making a match for my son in such a family
as yours, and that for nothing too!' 'No,' I cried, 'I'll never
have it.' 'Then it's my turn,' says he, and he walked away
scowling and left me. That was on Saturday last. On Monday I heard
from the lodge-keeper that he had been to the Pool. I knew what
was coming, and I knew what his coming meant. It meant that he
would be back in his old way, and I determined that it should be
for the last time. My disease had gained so much upon me that I
was desperate and cared little for my own life, if only I could
save Alice's from such a connection as that. I took my gun and I
strolled down to the wood, and I saw them talking. They had a
quarrel, and I heard the father tell the son that he should have
Alice or that he would have nothing more to do with him. Then the
son left him and walked away, and I saw McCarthy stand there with
his back towards me, and then I took a stone and I rushed at him
and struck him with all my strength. I remember his turning half
round as he fell, and then I heard the son's cry, and I ran away
behind the tree. But I must have dropped my cloak in my haste,
for I had to return for it, and it was only by God's mercy that
young McCarthy did not see me as he knelt by the body. And now I
have told you all, and you may do what you like with it."

"It would have been better for me to have gone into a gaol, or
into my grave, before I would have let my darling girl marry his
son. He came down to the Hall and swore it. He would have his own
way. Alice was to be the price of his silence. I knew she loved
the lad and would have had him if I had wished it, but I could
not allow it. I met him by the pool as we had arranged, and he
stood there among the trees, his wicked face close to mine, and
his breath hot on my cheek as he told me his will. Then I struck
him down. There was no need to strike twice, though I did. He fell
dead at my feet, and I, thinking of Alice and of the shame that
would come upon her, could not bring myself to give myself up. I
fled as best I could. You can think what I have suffered since."
He was gasping and ashen in the face as he spoke, and he pressed
his hand upon his side as though in pain. 

"I have done my best to clear the lad, but I could not do it
without ruining my own child," he continued. "You will not use
this confession, Mr. Holmes, unless you must?"

"I have already told you that I will not," answered Holmes. "I
shall only use it in case of necessity."

"Then I may go?"

"Yes, you may go."

"The very thought of her being the wife of that villain, even if
she were to be his son's, and not his own, was more than I could
bear. I told him so. Then he would not hear reason, he would have
nothing but his way. I had a word or two with him over this, and
he said he would wait a bit and think it over. Then he came to
Hatherley to ask for Alice's hand. I was waiting for him at the
pool and when he came up I told him I would not have it. He was
very angry and called me names, and I, too, was angry. Then he
told me he would go to the police and tell them all. He said he
would have me hanged. I could not bear to think of my Alice, and
how it would break her heart, so I hit him with a stone. I didn't
mean to kill him, but my blow was hard. When I saw what I had
done I ran away, but I remembered my cloak, so I went back for
it. Then I saw his son, and I was afraid. I didn't want him to
see me. I hid behind a tree, and I saw him with his father. He
cried and was very sad, and I felt bad for him. But I was more
afraid for my Alice, so I didn't say anything. I went home and I
have been very ill ever since. This is the truth, and I will sign
it."

"You see, his son was a handsome, high-spirited young man, and
McCarthy senior was a very ambitious man. He was determined that
his son should marry my girl and be master of my Hall. He knew
that he could make me do what he would, and he used his knowledge
to the very utmost. But I was not going to have that. Alice is
all I have. I've done everything for her; I've almost sold my
soul to make her happy. She should not marry a man she did not
love, and whose father I knew to be a villain. I told McCarthy
this, and we had a rare old row about it. It was then that he
threatened to tell everything to Alice, and I told him to do his
worst. But I knew that he would not, for it would mean his losing
his hold on me.

"But then he began to use his son as a tool. The young man, as I've
already told you, was a high-spirited fellow, and I've always
felt a liking for him, but he was under his father's thumb.
McCarthy senior would go to him and tell him that I had promised
my daughter's hand to him, and that he must go and press his
suit. Then the young man would come to me, and I'd have to put
him off with one excuse after another, while his father would
stand by and grin.

"Last Monday I went down to the pool to see McCarthy and have it
out with him once for all. I had my grey cloak on, for I had a
touch of the rheumatics, and I carried a heavy stick which I
often use when I'm walking. As I got near the pool I saw McCarthy
standing by the edge, and I heard him call 'Cooee!' to his son.
Then I saw the young man come up, and I heard them having a
quarrel. I stood behind a tree and listened, and I heard McCarthy
senior tell his son that he must marry Alice, and that if he
didn't he'd have him turned out of the house. The young man was
furious, and he told his father that he'd never marry her, and
then he turned and walked away.

"When he was gone I stepped out and faced McCarthy. He was
standing there with a look of triumph on his face, but it
changed to one of fear when he saw me. 'You've heard, have you?'
he said. 'Well, what are you going to do about it?'

"'I'm going to kill you,' I said, and I meant it too.

"I struck him a blow on the head with my stick, and he fell like
a log. I didn't mean to kill him, but I was mad with rage, and I

"That's the truth of the matter, Mr. Holmes. I've told you

Old Turner sank back on the sofa, his face ghastly white, and his
eyes closed. Sherlock Holmes sat in silence for a few minutes,
his chin on his hand, and his eyes fixed on the fire. At last he
rose and went over to the old man.

"I shall not give you up," he said. "You are a dying man, and I
cannot see that any good would come of your being arrested.
Young McCarthy will be acquitted, for I have evidence enough to
clear him. You can go home and spend your remaining days in
peace, and I promise you that your secret will be safe with me."

The old man looked up at him with a look of gratitude in his
eyes, and then he rose and limped from the room.

"Well, Watson," said Holmes as the door closed behind him, "that
was a strange case, was it not? It just shows you how easily
circumstantial evidence can lead one astray."

"It does indeed," I replied. "But what about the rat?"

"Ah, that was a little mistake of mine," said Holmes with a
smile. "I thought it was Ballarat, but it was really just a
rat. McCarthy senior was trying to tell his son that he'd seen a
rat running across the grass just before he was struck down. It
was a small detail, but it was enough to lead me to the truth."

And so the Boscombe Valley mystery was solved, and young James
McCarthy was acquitted of the murder of his father. Alice Turner
never knew the truth about her father's past, and she and James
were married a few months later. As for Sherlock Holmes, he
returned to London, ready for his next case.
